title: Lexicographically Smallest Palindrome
statement:
The string `s` contains only lowercase English letters. An operation overwrites one character of `s` with any lowercase letter of your choice.

Turn `s` into a palindrome (a string equal to its own reverse) using as few operations as possible. Among all palindromes reachable with that smallest number of operations, return the one that is lexicographically smallest, meaning that at the first index where two candidates differ, it has the letter that comes earlier in the alphabet.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

In a palindrome, index `i` and its mirror `n - 1 - i` must hold the same letter. Each mirror pair is independent of the others, so look at them one at a time. A pair that already matches costs nothing and should be left alone. A pair that differs needs at least one change, and one change is enough: copy one letter onto the other. To keep the operation count minimal we must pick one of the two existing letters, and picking the smaller one makes the string smaller at the left position without affecting any other pair. A brute force could try both choices for every mismatched pair, but that is exponential.

## Approach

1. Copy `s` into an array `chars` so letters can be overwritten.
2. Put `left` at the start and `right` at the end.
3. While `left < right`, compare `chars[left]` and `chars[right]`.
4. If they differ, write the `smaller` of the two into both positions.
5. Move both pointers inward. A middle character of an odd-length string is never touched.
6. Join `chars` back into a string.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "egcfe"`:

- `left = 0`, `right = 4`: `e` and `e` match, nothing changes.
- `left = 1`, `right = 3`: `g` and `f` differ; `smaller = "f"`, so both become `f`.
- `left = 2`, `right = 2`: the pointers meet at the middle `c`, so the loop stops.

The result is `"efcfe"`, made with one operation.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each mirror pair is examined once.
- Space: O(n) for the character array (strings are immutable in JavaScript).

## Pitfalls

- Do not replace a mismatched pair with `"a"`: that costs two operations instead of one, so it is not minimal.
- Leave matching pairs alone, even if both letters are large; changing them adds operations.
- Stop at `left < right`: the middle letter of an odd-length string never needs changing.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chars` | editable copy of `s` that becomes the palindrome |
| `left`, `right` | indices of the current mirror pair, moving toward the middle |
| `smaller` | the alphabetically earlier letter of a mismatched pair |

narration.2: Strings cannot be edited in place, so work on an array of characters.
narration.3: left starts at the first character...
narration.4: ...and right at its mirror, the last character.
narration.6: Process mirror pairs until the pointers meet in the middle.
narration.7: A matching pair already fits a palindrome; only a mismatch needs an operation.
narration.8: One change suffices, and keeping the earlier letter makes the string smallest.
narration.9: Write the smaller letter on the left side...
narration.10: ...and on the right side, so the pair now matches.
narration.12: Move left one step toward the middle.
narration.13: Move right one step toward the middle.
narration.15: Every pair matches now; join the characters into the answer.
